name: Battle of the Trebia
info: Hannibal's Carthaginian army lured a Roman army under the consul Sempronius Longus across the icy Trebia near Placentia in December 218 BCE, in the first major battle of the Second Punic War, and defeated it heavily.

facts.date: 22 or 23 December 218 BCE; the sources do not settle which
facts.place: The flood plain on the west bank of the lower Trebia river, not far from Placentia (modern Piacenza), in Cisalpine Gaul, northern Italy
facts.sides: Rome under the consul Sempronius Longus, with about 40,000 men (Polybius gives 16,000 Romans and Livy 18,000, with about 20,000 allied infantry and 4,000 cavalry); Carthage under Hannibal, about 40,000 men (29,000 infantry and 11,000 cavalry, with about 30 elephants)
facts.outcome: A heavy Roman defeat: most Roman units collapsed and most Romans were killed or captured, but about 10,000 under Sempronius kept formation and reached Placentia. Gallic recruits then joined Hannibal.

t: Each army had about 40,000 men; the Carthaginians were stronger in cavalry and the Romans in infantry, and Hannibal chose a flat flood plain where his cavalry could be used to greatest effect.
Hannibal used his Numidian cavalry to draw the Romans out before breakfast and across the chest-high, icy river, while 2,000 men under his brother Mago lay hidden in an old watercourse.
After the battle Gallic recruits flocked to Hannibal and his army grew to 60,000, and in spring 217 BCE he moved south into Roman Italy.
dyk: Sempronius sent his army across the Trebia in three columns, each 4 kilometres long, through water running chest-high on a cold, snowy morning, and few of his men are thought to have eaten breakfast.
ev: Hannibal besieges, captures and sacks Saguntum, and Rome declares war on Carthage
Hannibal crosses the Alps and enters what is now Piedmont
The Carthaginian cavalry beats the Romans at the Ticinus, and Publius Scipio is wounded
Sempronius brings his army from Sicily to join Scipio on the Trebia
Hannibal draws the Romans across the Trebia and defeats them (on 22 or 23 December)
The Carthaginians are recognised as the dominant force in Cisalpine Gaul and their army grows to 60,000
Hannibal crosses the Apennines and defeats the Romans at Lake Trasimene
Hannibal marches to southern Italy and wins the Battle of Cannae

sections.background:
The First Punic War, fought from 264 to 241 BCE, ended with Carthage defeated after 23 years. Five years later Hamilcar Barca landed in Carthaginian Iberia and made it a quasi-monarchical, autonomous territory ruled by his family, the Barcids. It gave Carthage silver mines, agricultural wealth, manpower and shipyards, which encouraged it to resist future Roman demands. Hannibal succeeded his father-in-law Hasdrubal in 221 BCE, and in 219 BCE his army besieged, captured and sacked Saguntum, a city with a treaty of association with Rome. Rome declared war on Carthage.

In 218 BCE Rome raised an army for Iberia under the consul Publius Scipio. The Gallic tribes of Cisalpine Gaul, antagonised by Roman colonists settled at Placentia and Cremona on Gallic land, rose and attacked the Romans. The Senate took a Roman and an allied legion from the Iberian force to send to the region, so the Scipios could not set out until September. Hannibal marched from Iberia in May, crossed the Rhone and then the Alps in October, and came down into what is now Piedmont with 20,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and about 30 elephants. He needed food and Gallic allies, so he stormed the capital of the unwelcoming Taurini and massacred its population as a message to the other tribes.

Publius Scipio, back in Italy, led the cavalry and light infantry of his army against the Carthaginians at the Ticinus, where the Romans were soundly beaten and Scipio was wounded. The Romans retreated to Placentia, and then to high ground by the Trebia at what is now Rivergaro, to await reinforcement.
sections.forces:
The consul Sempronius Longus had been assembling an army in western Sicily for an invasion of Africa the next year. The Senate ordered it north, and it reached Ariminum (modern Rimini) after 40 days, probably part of the way by sea. It joined Scipio's army on the Trebia, and because Scipio was still partly incapacitated by his wounds Sempronius took overall command.

The Roman force had four Roman legions, which at full strength should have mustered 16,800 men including 4,800 velites, though at least one was significantly understrength. Polybius gives 16,000 Romans and Livy, writing 200 years later, 18,000. There were also about 20,000 allied infantry, four Latin legions and a strong force of Gauls, and 4,000 cavalry of Romans, Latins and Gauls. Mention is made of 6,000 light infantry, which most modern historians take to be included in the 36,000 or 38,000 infantry.

Hannibal had 29,000 infantry, 21,000 of them close-order and 8,000 light, and 11,000 cavalry, a mixture of Africans, Iberians and Gauls; 8,000 of the close-order infantry were Gauls, and the other proportions are not known. He also had about 30 elephants, survivors of the 37 with which he had left Iberia. Carthage recruited foreigners, many from North Africa and called Libyans, so the army's strength was in cavalry and skirmishers, and he preferred to fight on the flat, open flood plain, where his cavalry could manoeuvre. Sempronius wanted a battle before Scipio recovered and before new consuls took office in less than three months.
sections.course:
On the night before, Hannibal sent his younger brother Mago with 1,000 cavalry and 1,000 infantry to hide in an old watercourse full of brush south of the field. The morning of 22 or 23 December was cold and snowy. Before daybreak Hannibal sent Numidian cavalry across the river to push back the Roman pickets and provoke a fight, while the rest of his army ate an early breakfast. Sempronius sent out all his cavalry, then his 6,000 velites, and finally his whole army, in three columns each 4 kilometres long, across the Trebia, which was running chest-high. Few, if any, of his men had eaten.

The Carthaginian army formed symmetrically: 8,000 Gallic infantry in the centre, 6,000 African and Iberian veterans on each side, half of the elephants beyond each of these and 5,000 cavalry on each wing. The Romans put their heavy infantry in the centre, perhaps 13,000 strong, with about 17,000 allies on the flanks and cavalry on the wings. The Carthaginian light infantry, fully supplied and with slingers who outranged the velites, drove the cold, hungry velites back.

On each wing 5,000 Carthaginian cavalry met 2,000 Roman, and both contests were quickly decided, the Romans fleeing back over the river. The Carthaginian light infantry then moved round the exposed Roman flanks, and the Roman allied infantry turned to face them. Mago's 2,000 came down the watercourse into the Roman left rear. Part of the Roman line broke, but the Roman centre routed the 8,000 Gauls and an African unit and broke through, only to find the rest of the army dissolved. Sempronius led 10,000 back across the river to Placentia.
sections.aftermath:
Modern historians debate the Roman losses. Dexter Hoyos states that the only survivors were the infantry who broke through the Carthaginian centre, and Richard Miles says that many of those outside this group were killed. Goldsworthy says the Romans suffered heavily but that numbers of soldiers straggled into Placentia or the camps. John Lazenby argues that, outside a group of 12,500, few infantry escaped but most of the cavalry did. According to Paul Erdkamp the Romans lost 20,000 killed, half of their force, not counting the captured. Carthaginian losses are generally agreed to have been several thousand of the Gallic infantry in the centre, fewer of their other infantry and cavalry, and several elephants. Many African infantry were re-equipped with captured Roman armour and weapons.

The wounded Scipio gathered the guards left in the camps and marched to Placentia. News of the defeat caused panic in Rome, which calmed once Sempronius arrived to preside over the consular elections. Gnaeus Servilius Geminus and Gaius Flaminius were chosen, and the Carthaginian cavalry isolated Placentia and Cremona, which could be supplied by boat up the Po. The consuls-elect raised further legions, reinforced Sardinia and Sicily, garrisoned Tarentum, built a fleet of 60 quinqueremes and set up supply depots at Ariminum and Arretium. Two armies of four legions each were formed, one at Arretium and one on the Adriatic coast.
sections.sources:
Polybius, a near-contemporary Greek historian, and Livy, who wrote about 200 years later, are the sources the modern accounts rest on, and they differ. Polybius gives the Roman force as 16,000 Romans and Livy as 18,000. Polybius holds that after the battle the Carthaginians were recognised as the dominant force in Cisalpine Gaul and that most Gallic tribes sent supplies and recruits, so that the army grew to 60,000. Livy claims the Carthaginians suffered from a shortage of food throughout the winter and gives dramatic accounts of winter confrontations, which Goldsworthy describes as probably an invention.

Much is uncertain. The date is 22 or 23 December. The sources are unclear whether the 6,000 light infantry are part of the infantry totals, how many Gauls fought with the Romans and where they stood, and whether the elephants carried towers. Roman losses are debated, from the view that the only survivors were the formed group that broke through to the view that many stragglers and most of the cavalry also escaped, and the size of that group is put at 10,000 or 12,500.
sections.legacy:
The Trebia was the first major battle of the Second Punic War and a heavy defeat for Rome. It confirmed the Carthaginians as the dominant force in Cisalpine Gaul, and Gallic recruits flocked to Hannibal. The Roman army in Sicily, which had been meant for Africa, had been drawn north and beaten, and the Senate's response was to raise new legions and a fleet and to guard Sardinia, Sicily and the south.

In spring 217 BCE, probably early May, Hannibal crossed the Apennines unopposed by a difficult but unguarded route. He cut the supply line of the consul Gaius Flaminius to Rome, provoked him into a hasty pursuit and set an ambush, and at the Battle of Lake Trasimene he surprised and completely defeated the Romans, killing Flaminius and another 15,000 Romans and taking 15,000 prisoner.

In 216 BCE Hannibal marched to southern Italy and won the Battle of Cannae, which Richard Miles describes as Rome's greatest military disaster. Toni Ñaco del Hoyo describes the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae as the three great military calamities suffered by the Romans in the first three years of the war. The Carthaginians campaigned in southern Italy for a further 13 years. In 204 BCE the younger Publius Cornelius Scipio, the son of the Scipio wounded at the Ticinus, invaded the Carthaginian homeland, and Hannibal was recalled and defeated at Zama in October 202 BCE, after which Carthage agreed a peace that stripped it of most of its territory and power.

summary: At the Trebia in December 218 BCE Hannibal drew Sempronius's army across an icy river and, with cavalry, light infantry and a hidden force, defeated it heavily; 10,000 Romans reached Placentia. Gallic recruits joined Hannibal, and the war moved on to Lake Trasimene and Cannae.
references: John Lazenby, Hannibal's War: A Military History of the Second Punic War (Aris & Phillips, 1998)
Adrian Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage: The Punic Wars 265–146 BC (Phoenix, 2006)
Dexter Hoyos, Mastering the West: Rome and Carthage at War (Oxford University Press, 2015)
Nigel Bagnall, The Punic Wars: Rome, Carthage and the Struggle for the Mediterranean (Pimlico, 1999)
Richard Miles, Carthage Must be Destroyed (Penguin, 2011)
notes: The article gives the Roman survivors as 10,000 in its lead and prose but Lazenby's group as 12,500; both are given.
Hannibal's 'thinning' of the line and the elephants' purpose were left out of the course for length.
Facts 'sides' strengths: the 40,000 each is the lead's 'about 40,000'; the totals 29,000 plus 11,000 are the article's.
The article says Romans had about 30,000 heavy infantry to the Carthaginians' 20,000 but also 21,000 close-order Carthaginian infantry; I left the comparison out.
The article calls Sempronius's cavalry force before the battle 'large, but of unknown size'; the skirmish of the prelude was left out for length.
Left out: the Gauls beheading Romans at the Roman camp, the Clastidium grain depot, the generals' speeches.
The article gives no legacy or memory beyond the war itself; the legacy section covers the war's sequel.
